item.title: Newsom's death penalty gamble could help him in 2028 — or come back to bite him
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A view of the East Block of San Quentin Rehab Center's death row, which was shut down by Gov. Gavin Newsom earlier in his term before he announced Thursday that he was commuting the sentences of condemned inmates. (Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times) While running for California governor in 2018, Gavin Newsom declared that he would rather be bold and fail than retreat to the safety of mediocrity. The two-term governor known for taking big political risks once again made good on that vow Thursday when he moved to offer clemency to every inmate sentenced to death in California. Amid a hum of speculation about how the mass commutation could help or hurt his presidential prospects in 2028, the Democratic politician sent a clear, defining message to Americans about where he stands and the type of leader they could expect. “If my job is just to read the polls, you can have an AI chatbot as governor,” Newsom said in an interview Friday. “I was hired for my judgment, and like it or hate it, that was why I think I was given this privilege, and that’s the responsibility of a leader. My job’s leadership, not stewardship. It’s not management. It’s to lead. “I’m here to change polls, change minds.” The sweeping decision comes more than 20 years after Newsom emerged in the national consciousness when, as mayor of San Francisco, he defied federal law and allowed same-sex marriages in the City by the Bay. California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks at the "Stop the Power Grab rally" at the Hollywood Palladium in Los Angeles on Nov. 1, 2026. (Ariana Drehsler / For The Times) Bold moves that test the limits of his power, such as a controversial, first-in-the-nation stay-at-home order during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic and spearheading Proposition 50 last year to redraw California’s congressional districts to offset Republican attempts to gerrymander red states, have defined his leadership, for good or bad. The Democratic governor said those kinds of decisions are “sort of embedded in my DNA.” About a decade ago he said he was pushed to describe his core motivation. Though he admits it sounds trite, the governor said: “It’s to stand up for ideals and strike out against injustice.” The death penalty, he said, is not handed out equally. He quoted Bryan Stevenson, the founder of Equal Justice Initiative, who said you’re better off being rich and guilty than poor and innocent. “I couldn’t not have done this,” Newsom said. “There was an easy out, but ... I would the rest of my life felt, you know, ashamed of myself.” Commuting the death sentences of all 548 state prisoners awaiting execution pushes the bounds of his authority once again. California voters have twice rejected ballot measures to abolish the death penalty , first in 2012 and again in 2016, and Newsom’s decision overrides the will of the courts and state laws that permit capital punishment. Read more: Newsom moves to commute all California death sentences to life in prison without parole Under the state Constitution, Newsom has the power to commute about 40% of the death sentences on his own. The rest of the cases, which involve prisoners who had a felony conviction on their record prior to receiving a death sentence, or racked up additional crimes while awaiting execution, require approval from the California Supreme Court — a constitutional check to ensure the governor’s actions are not an abuse of power. The court rejected 10 commutations handed out by Gov. Jerry Brown in his last full month in office — all of which involved people convicted of multiple felonies — and did not provide an explanation for the action. Despite Newsom’s push to commute all death sentences, capital punishment remains legal in California and prosecutors can continue seeking that punishment. Los Angeles County Dist. Atty. Nathan Hochman speaks during a news conference at the Hall of Justice last month. (Ronaldo Bolaños / Los Angeles Times) Los Angeles County Dist. Atty. Nathan Hochman said until the law is changed, his office “will continue to evaluate every death penalty-eligible case with the rigor, care and restraint these decisions demand.” Sacramento County Sheriff Jim Cooper urged Newsom to reconsider the commutations. He said he remembers watching Luis Bracamontes, who was sentenced to death for killing Sacramento County Sheriff’s Deputy Danny Oliver and Placer County Sheriff’s Detective Michael Davis Jr. in 2014, “laugh in court while their families, including Danny’s two young daughters, had to sit and watch. “Deputy Danny Oliver and Detective Michael Davis Jr. should be alive today, enjoying long and healthy lives with their families,” Cooper said in a statement. “Instead, the man who murdered them has now escaped his sentence.” Others accused the governor of reducing the death penalty sentences to seek an advantage in the 2028 presidential election. “The people of California deserve leaders who put politics and personal ambition aside and pursue truth, accountability, and justice with courage, integrity, and transparency,” said Michael Hestrin, Riverside County district attorney, in a statement. “Instead they have been presented with a decision that demonstrates a profound disregard for the victims, their families, and the prosecutors who dedicated themselves to seeking justice on their behalf.” Luis Bracamontes looks up in Sacramento Superior Court in 2018 as the verdict is read in the killing of two law enforcement officers. Bracamontes was found guilty. (Rich Pedroncelli / Associated Press) A poll conducted in August by the Pew Research Center found that about two-thirds of voters nationally favor the death penalty for people convicted of murder. Political analysts suggest that reducing the sentences adds to Newsom’s credentials as a progressive leader and aligns him with Democratic primary voters on the issue if he runs for president. Republicans, however, could take advantage of Newsom’s action and cast him as a soft-on-crime liberal who is out of touch with most Americans, which risks turning away moderate voters. But others cautioned that national political elections are hard to predict. Gar Culbert, chair of the political science department at Cal State Los Angeles, said it would be politically advantageous for Newsom to try to appeal to the Democratic Party’s base as he considers a run for president. Culbert said he doesn’t believe the death penalty will be a substantial issue in a general election when, if Newsom becomes the Democratic presidential nominee, his Republican challenger would attack his record as California governor regardless. “It’s possible he’s not being strategic,” Culbert said. “Maybe he doesn’t have to be strategic because he just might think it’s the right thing to do.” The governor first issued a moratorium on executions about two months after he took office in 2019, saying capital punishment is discriminatory and unjust. Without the moratorium, 45 people would be subject to execution now, according to his office. Daniel Zingale worked for Newsom as a senior advisor in the governor’s office at the start of his first term. Part of Zingale’s job at the time was to consider how the governor’s actions would be received by the public. “The only piece of data he was not interested in in that process were the polls,” Zingale said. “His view, and I agree with this, is this is not an issue that you can leverage politically.” Read more: Gov. Gavin Newsom to block California death row executions, close San Quentin execution chamber Newsom’s decision to commute the sentences won’t have much practical effect in a state that has not executed a prisoner since 2006. At Newsom’s command, the death chamber was dismantled at San Quentin State Prison, now San Quentin Rehabilitation Center, after he issued his moratorium. His successor, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, has also said he will continue the pause on executions. There was no immediate need to offer commutations to save the lives of the inmates. Taking no action would have been the safe bet, Newsom said in an interview about his decision a day after he made the announcement. Many people around him, he said, advised him to do nothing. He also understands that commuting the sentences could make him vulnerable if he runs for president. “I’m not an idiot. The ads write themselves,” Newsom said. “But I just also would be fake. I wouldn’t be myself and if I’m going to be up there and not be myself, I couldn’t do that.” With the clock ticking on his time in office, the governor said he also doesn’t want to leave with regrets. “I don’t want to be one of the elders on some panel talking about what I would have, could have, should have done,” Newsom said. “I’ve spent my life trying not to be that person. I’ve been willing to take risks. I’ve been willing to go first on so many issues. “If others aren’t willing to do it, you know what? I’ll raise my hand, and I’m happy, honestly, to take the hits.” Sign up for Essential California for news, features and recommendations from the L.A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times . This article originally appeared on LA Times at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/death-sentence-clemency-newsom-takes-032948182.html

item.title: Stephen Miller pushed for 3,000 ICE arrests a day. Now he's Trump's chief of staff.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — Top Trump adviser Stephen Miller , who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, has driven President Trump's most controversial immigration policies during both of his administrations. Mr. Trump announced the staffing shake-up on Friday, calling Miller one of his "most trusted" advisers. Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who has been his chief of staff throughout his second term. The move comes after Republicans suffered crippling losses in the midterm elections and as Democrats plan sweeping investigations into the administration's actions, including its immigration enforcement policies. Miller was the architect behind many of those policies and also championed the administration's immigration enforcement expansion, which has been supported by approximately $170 billion that congressional Republicans allocated for immigration enforcement and border security in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which became law in July 2025. During Mr. Trump's first term, Miller helped develop and publicly defend the administration's executive order that restricted entry by nationals of several Muslim-majority countries. The travel ban led to protests around the U.S. and legal challenges. A third iteration of the ban was upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018. He was a leading supporter of the administration's 2018 zero-tolerance immigration policy, which resulted in thousands of family separations, and he pressed for dramatic reductions in refugee admissions. The administration repeatedly lowered the annual refugee admissions ceiling, ultimately setting it at 15,000 for fiscal year 2021, a record low at the time. Under former President Barack Obama, the ceiling was 110,000 for fiscal year 2017. Miller also advocated penalizing legal immigrants who received public benefits and making it harder for them to obtain citizenship. In Mr. Trump's second term, Miller pushed Immigration and Customs Enforcement to make at least 3,000 immigration arrests per day. In May 2025, Miller publicly demanded a dramatic increase in daily arrests, placing pressure on ICE leadership and expanding enforcement beyond immigrants who had been convicted of serious crimes. He also proposed that the National Guard be deployed to support mass deportations. Miller's arrest targets were part of a sweeping expansion of enforcement in communities, workplaces and immigration courts. Detentions of immigrants without criminal histories rose sharply , and increased ICE activity sparked protests across the country. The longtime Trump adviser also championed the use of a wartime law — the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 — to bypass due process and quickly deport alleged Venezuelan gang members to El Salvador, where they were held in a notorious maximum-security prison, known as CECOT. The deportations set off a legal battle, and the Supreme Court blocked the government from immediately deporting the Venezuelans without giving them an opportunity to challenge their removal. As part of the administration's deportation efforts, Miller has supported an aggressive expansion of third-country deportations . The administration has deported immigrants to countries where they have no citizenship or family ties, including several African nations . In May 2025, Miller said the administration was actively considering suspending the constitutional mechanism that allows detainees to challenge their confinement in court. At a March 2026 conference in Miami, Miller argued that military force, rather than traditional criminal law enforcement alone, was needed to defeat cartels. Miller appeared alongside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office this summer as he signed executive orders to refuse citizenship to some children born in the United States, after the Supreme Court struck down his earlier executive order aiming to end birthright citizenship. item.title: Elizabeth Warren's new Senate role puts Wall Street and Trump on notice for hearings
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democratic firebrand Elizabeth Warren, a consumer advocate known for her fierce battles over financial regulations, will take the gavel in January to become chair of the powerful Senate Banking Committee. According to a source familiar with her plans, the Massachusetts senator intends to use her expanded platform to advance legislation to tackle populist affordability issues with a focus on housing. The person familiar with her plans says Warren will use the committee's investigative powers to hold hearings and launch investigations into executive branch ethics and corporate practices, aiming to hold President Trump, the administration, Wall Street, and Big Tech accountable for economic decisions she views as having driven up costs for consumers. Warren is also expected to take steps to shield the Federal Reserve from White House overreach . Any future nominee for the Fed will have to go through her committee. Earlier this year, she rallied Democrats to oppose Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's confirmation before the banking committee, stalling his eventual confirmation. Wall Street is likely to be another of Warren's targets. Before Republicans regained control of Congress, Democrats would have the chief executives of big banks testify before the Senate Banking and House Financial Services committees once a year. The banking industry can expect a return to that practice. Stephen Biggar, who covers the financial sector for Argus Research, says hearings will offer more transparency, but won't be accompanied by meaningful rulemaking. Biggar expects increased oversight, potentially more consumer protections, and actions to limit banks' market share size, such as blocking mergers. He added that there are concerns that the deregulation efforts and lower capital requirements for banks championed by Republicans are now at risk. James Angel, an associate professor at Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business, said he thinks the hearings will accomplish two things: producing information and sound bites that will get people to pay attention and galvanize public opinion. Second, Angel says they will serve as a deterrent for people in power. "If people will be held under oath and there's a prospect of perjury, that will deter people from doing 'Trumpier' things," Angel said in an interview. Angel also noted that any Trump appointee who has to be confirmed by Warren's committee will need to withstand bipartisan scrutiny and thus is more likely to be a moderate. Prediction markets, housing, AI, and credit card rates This summer, Warren teamed up with current Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott to pass a sprawling bipartisan housing bill that addresses housing affordability by encouraging more homebuilding, expanding financing options, and restricting large corporate investors buying single-family homes. Warren is expected to continue her push to rein in private equity across industries that she sees jacking up costs for families. Warren also intends to conduct oversight into prediction markets and election betting platforms to prevent insider trading and platform manipulation. Before the midterm elections, Warren co-authored a letter with Utah Sen. John Curtis to executives of Kalshi and Polymarket asking them to explain how they would prevent candidates, campaign staff, and others with inside information from trading on election contracts. There are also potential areas of common ground with Republicans, including advancing bipartisan AI export-control bills. Warren worked on three such bills this year, including a measure to stop advanced AI chips from being used by China to develop dangerous systems. One area of agreement that could secure Trump's signature: capping credit card interest rates. It's something both Warren and Trump support, along with newly elected Democrats, including Texas's new senator, James Talarico. Follow Jennifer Schonberger on X @Jenniferisms and on Instagram . This article originally appeared on Yahoo Finance at https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/elizabeth-warren-will-take-over-the-senate-banking-committee-next-year-expect-hearings-205713342.html

item.title: Latino vote helped thwart Texas Republicans' redistricting effort
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Last year, the Republican-controlled Texas legislature redrew its congressional maps in a controversial mid-decade redistricting effort aimed at giving the GOP five more House seats. Encouraged by President Donald Trump's strong showing among Hispanic voters in 2024, they concentrated on four districts in the heavily Latino Rio Grande Valley in South Texas. But the Latino vote in Texas swung back from the president on Tuesday, driven by its dissatisfaction with Trump's immigration policy and the economy, according to ABC News' Voter Poll. Republicans failed to flip any of the Rio Grand Valley districts -- losing by double-digits in all of them -- and ended up with a net loss of one House seat. Hispanic voters comprise more than 30% of eligible Texas voters and are especially concentrated in four counties in the Rio Grande Valley, where they make up more than 90% of the population, according to U.S. census data. Brandon Bell/Getty Images - PHOTO: Democrats candidate for House Bobby Pulido, Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa sing together at the conclusion of the Voto Latino's "Ready. Go. Vote." campaign rally, Oct. 25, 2026 in Weslaco, Texas. ABC News' Voter Poll showed 67% of Hispanics who voted in the state's Senate race said the Trump administration's actions on immigration enforcement have gone too far, compared to 45% of white Senate voters. Who won the redistricting war? So far, it looks like Democrats Jon Taylor, a University of Texas at San Antonio political science professor, told ABC affiliate KSAT that this issue is especially influential in the Rio Grande Valley saying, "A number of people living in South Texas, living in San Antonio, who had family, friends, somebody they knew who got picked up in an ICE raid. It had a profound impact on voting." About 83% of Hispanic voters said the economy was not so good or poor, compared to 63% of white voters, according to ABC News' Voter Poll, and 75% of Hispanics who voted in the Senate race said that Trump's economic policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S., compared to 52% of white voters. The Rio Grande Valley has some of the highest rates of poverty in the country. Héctor E. Sánchez Barba, who leads Mi Familia Vota, a leading Latino political group, told ABC News that the Valley has been particularly hurt by the Trump's economic policies, saying "It's very clear the economic impact that these policies are having is on mostly working-class, people-of-color communities." All four of the Rio Grande Valley counties saw voter turnout up from 2022: Up 9.9% in Hidalgo County; 7.9% higher in Cameron County; a 7.4% increase in Willacy County; and 3.3% higher in Starr County. The state saw an overall increase of about 6% in voter turnout from 2022. Brandon Bell/Getty Images - PHOTO: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks during a campaign rally at the Santa Fe Event Center, Oct. 25, 2026, in Weslaco, Texas. Additionally, Democrats flipped two largely Hispanic districts in South Texas that Trump had previously won by double digit margins. And the blue wave extended to Democrats winning all statewide races. ABC News Voter polls showed that Hispanic voters backed Democratic Senate Candidate James Talarico with 68% of the vote and Democratic governor candidate Gina Hinojosa with 65%. Barba said they won because "Their policies are a reflection of working class families" and a "reflection of inclusion." Barba said the Democratic victories could make the state a presidential battleground in 2028. "Make no mistake, anybody that wants to become a president in 2028 has to come through the Latino community." This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/latino-vote-helped-thwart-texas-republicans-redistricting-effort/story?id=137880812

item.title: Trump signals more cabinet changes in store after Republican midterm losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Hegseth and Miller (AP) President Donald Trump said Friday he expects to make additional Cabinet changes following Republicans' sweeping midterm election defeats, signaling that the replacement of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles may be only the beginning of a broader administration shake-up. In an interview with CBS News' "60 Minutes," Trump acknowledged that more personnel changes could be coming but declined to identify which officials might be affected. Asked whether he expected to fire anyone after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress, Trump replied, "I do, yeah. Little bit." "I love my Cabinet. I think they're good," Trump said. "But I'll ... be doing maybe a few changes." The remarks came as Trump announced Friday that longtime senior adviser Stephen Miller would replace Wiles as White House chief of staff, effective Monday. Trump's comments were made during an interview with CBS News correspondent Ross Douthat scheduled to air Sunday, with excerpts released Friday. The president's remarks also come amid growing speculation about the future of War Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose handling of the war in Iran has drawn criticism following the GOP's midterm losses. CBS News reported Wednesday that Trump had privately asked advisers whether Hegseth should remain in his position, citing multiple sources familiar with the discussions. The network reported that Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis had been floated as a possible replacement, although other sources said Trump had made no decision to remove Hegseth. Trump publicly expressed confidence in Hegseth when questioned Wednesday and again during the CBS interview. "I do," Trump replied Friday when asked whether he retained confidence in Hegseth. "Look, we've won two wars," the president added, referring to U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Iran. Hegseth also faces the prospect of intensified congressional scrutiny when Democrats take control of the House and Senate in January. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Friday that Hegseth should leave office but stopped short of endorsing impeachment proceedings, according to NPR. "He's got to go," Jeffries said during an interview with NPR's "Morning Edition." Asked whether Democrats should pursue impeachment, Jeffries replied, "I don't want to get out ahead of the caucus." NPR also reported that Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., has threatened to force a House vote on eight articles of impeachment unless Hegseth resigns. Meanwhile, Trump's decision to elevate Miller places one of his closest advisers in charge of White House operations as Democrats prepare to challenge administration policies and launch congressional investigations. CBS News reported Friday that Miller, previously deputy chief of staff, has played a central role in shaping Trump's immigration enforcement and deportation policies. His appointment could also set the stage for a more confrontational relationship with incoming Democrat congressional leaders, who have sharply criticized the administration's immigration agenda. Trump, however, rejected suggestions that Wiles' departure was prompted by the election results. "It's just time. Sometimes you change," Trump told reporters Friday, according to CNN. CBS News separately reported that Wiles submitted her resignation Thursday and that her departure was tied to the Republican election defeats, citing three sources familiar with the matter. Trump praised Miller as a trusted and effective adviser. "He's been with me right from the beginning ... he's very loyal, smart. Does a great job," Trump said, according to CNN. "He's been an MVP every year. He's been just great. So, we're very happy with him," the president added. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, has specifically identified Miller as a target for investigation. "Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct," Garcia said in a statement Friday reported by Mediaite. "Stephen Miller should lawyer up," Garcia added. CBS News also reported that Garcia had singled out Miller and other administration officials as potential investigative targets following Tuesday's elections. The White House has dismissed the prospect of such inquiries as politically motivated. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told CBS News. © 2026 Newsmax. item.title: Missiles target Kyiv and injure 5 people as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the U.S.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Missile attacks struck across Ukraine on Saturday, wounding at least nine people, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States. Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war . The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, the most recent having been in Geneva in February. Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved. The Russian missiles that hit overnight across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv , damaged homes and commercial properties, triggering new power and water outages, national and city authorities said. Kateryna Korniichuk, 64, was at home with her granddaughter when an attack hit. “The first blast wave threw us against that wall and then against the other wall, because we were in the corridor. It’s very hard. No sleep, no peace — nothing. The children aren’t sleeping, and neither are we," she told The Associated Press. “I’m old, I can handle it, but what have the children done wrong?” Strikes also prompted officials to close Kyiv's 816-meter-long (892-yard-long) Northern Bridge, a major route connecting the city with large residential areas on the east bank of the Dnipro River. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that work was already underway to repair the city's Northern Bridge and that water pressure in Kyiv had been stabilized. Earlier Saturday, he had described the city's energy situation as "extremely difficult, affecting the city’s heating and water supply systems.” Zelenskyy slams Russian attacks ahead of trilateral negotiations In a statement Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was preparing for trilateral talks by “launching ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s critical infrastructure.” The Ukrainian leader said that Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight. The barrage also involved 172 drones over Kyiv and 12 other regions, wounding nine people, including a child, he said. “When Russia tries to plunge Kyiv — a city of millions — and the entire country into a blackout, Ukraine must not be left to face this alone,” Zelenskyy said. He urged greater U.S. support and attention from Congress, calling for bipartisan backing for Ukraine and stronger sanctions on Russia. Ukraine’s Energy Ministry said Saturday’s missile attacks damaged networks that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central regions, as well as multiple other power facilities. It said outages were most widespread in the Kyiv and central Zhytomyr regions, as well as in the eastern regions of Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk. The outages were separate from scheduled rolling blackouts imposed to protect the grid, which remain in effect across much of Ukraine. Russia’s Ministry of Defense confirmed Saturday that it had targeted the Northern Bridge, saying that it facilitated the transport of weaponry, military hardware and specialist equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces. It also said that it had targeted an industrial facility in the capital producing Flamingo missiles, as well as a power station, an electrical substation, and a plant producing ammunition, explosives and gunpowder in the wider Kyiv region. It also confirmed striking an electrical substation in the Zhytomyr region. Death toll rises to 55 after the strike on aid center in Komyshuvakha Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued into its sixth day in the village of Komyshuvakha , devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid. Emergency services said they had recovered nine more bodies in the previous 24 hours, bringing the death toll early Saturday morning to 55. Dozens of people remain missing. Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, said he was still looking for his wife but had heard no word from rescuers. “She went to get humanitarian aid, and a three-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?” he said. “She didn’t come home, and they didn’t find her body there. She isn’t in the morgue, and she isn’t here alive.” The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region. Ukrainian attack on Russia's Belgorod region kills 1 person A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia’s Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said Saturday. Russia’s Ministry of Defense said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, it said. The head of Russia’s southwestern Saratov region, Gov. Roman Busargin, wrote on social media that a drone attack damaged “civilian infrastructure” and several residential buildings in the area. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city. The head of Russia’s Oryol region, Gov. Andrey Klychkov, also said Saturday that a Ukrainian attack had damaged commercial warehouse and production sites in the regional capital, as cited by state media. Russian media outlets reported that a Ukrainian attack sparked a blaze at Oryol’s Proton-Electrotex plant, which produces components for military equipment. ___ Dmytro Zhyhinas and Dan Bashakov in Kyiv, Ukraine, Vasilisa Stepanenko in Komyshuvakha, Ukraine, and Katie Marie Davies in Manchester, England, contributed to this report. ___ Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/missiles-target-kyiv-injure-5-072141209.html

item.title: Democrats' midterm wins could change how we elect presidents by 2028
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Could this year's big blue midterm wave transform how America elects its next president? Now that Democrats have won complete control of governor's mansions and both legislative chambers in five battleground states — Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada and Arizona — there is a chance that the Electoral College, as we know it, could soon become a thing of the past. That isn't speculation. In fact, the plan is already in motion. Over the last two decades, 18 states and Washington, D.C., have formally agreed to award all of their electoral votes to whichever presidential ticket wins the most votes nationwide, regardless of the outcome in their own state or district. Until now, this legal agreement — official name: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (NPVIC) — hasn't taken effect because the jurisdictions that have joined it only control 222 total electoral votes, which falls short of the 270 required to activate the compact (and elect a president). But what if you add Pennsylvania (19 electoral votes), Michigan (15), Arizona (11), Wisconsin (10) and Nevada (6) to the list? That gets you to 283 (assuming that all of them join and the compact survives potential constitutional challenges). Since Election Day, the Democratic shift in statehouses across the country has been overshadowed by the massive Democratic shift on Capitol Hill . But as the dust settles, attention is turning toward a new possibility: that a handful of states might suddenly have the power to ensure that whoever wins the national popular vote in 2028 will also win the presidency (which hasn't always been the case ). "The time is right," Carrie Rheingans, a Democrat in the Michigan House of Representatives, told the New York Times this week . "This blue tsunami is really going to help push this forward across the whole nation." "National popular vote will be something that we'll prioritize early in the session," added Kelda Roys, a Democratic state lawmaker in Wisconsin. Here's everything you need to know about the national popular vote compact — and its chances of taking effect. How does the Electoral College currently work? The Electoral College is a system of indirect democracy in which the winner of the U.S. presidential election is determined not by the combined number of votes a candidate has earned across all states — aka the "popular vote" — but rather by the number of "electoral votes" they've amassed by winning in individual states. With minor exceptions, the candidate who gets the most votes in a particular state on Election Day is awarded all of that state's electoral votes, which match the number of senators and representatives it sends to Congress. Whichever presidential ticket secures a majority of electoral votes — that is, 270 — wins. Due to the winner-take-all nature of the Electoral College, candidates tend not to campaign in states that consistently vote Democratic (blue states) or Republican (red states). Instead, they focus on the small number of states (known as swing states, battleground states, toss-up states or purple states) that could go one way or the other. The Founding Fathers established the Electoral College in the Constitution. Some of them wanted qualified citizens to elect the president by popular vote; others wanted Congress to elect the president. The Electoral College was the compromise they landed on. Today's Electoral College system evolved over time as individual states passed their own winner-take-all laws. But the Founders never specified how electors — the ones who cast the electoral votes — would be appointed. Instead, the Constitution explicitly delegates that power to the states themselves, saying they can choose their electors "in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct." National popular vote advocates argue that this clause gives state lawmakers " a built-in way to reform the system ." How could the national popular vote compact change America's presidential elections? Prior to the 20th century, three presidents won the White House without winning the popular vote: John Quincy Adams in 1824, Rutherford B. Hayes in 1876 and Benjamin Harrison in 1888. But the idea for a national popular vote compact only started to gain traction among scholars after George W. Bush lost the popular vote in 2000 and wound up in the White House anyway. Sixteen years later, Trump's popular-vote loss to Hillary Clinton — by a margin of nearly 3 million ballots — added more fuel to the fire. The Bush and Trump victories also polarized the issue, making Democrats more open to the idea of reform — and Republicans more opposed (in general). The NPVIC was introduced in 2006 by John Koza , a computer scientist and former Democratic elector who co-invented the lottery scratchcard. The idea is simple. First, individual states agree to award all of their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote. When enough states agree — that is, enough states with a combined total of at least 270 electoral votes — then the compact will take effect and the candidate who earns the most popular votes nationwide will be guaranteed enough electoral votes to win the White House. No constitutional amendment required. National popular vote proponents say that their plan will completely change the way candidates campaign for (and even govern as) president. Rather than lavishing all their time, energy and resources on a small handful of swing states, aspiring commanders in chief would in theory have to cater to voters everywhere in hopes of maximizing their nationwide vote tally. In April 2007, Maryland became the first state to sign on. Ten more jurisdictions followed suit before the 2016 election (California, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington and the District of Columbia), with another eight joining the compact after Trump became president (Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Minnesota, New Mexico, Oregon and Virginia). Republican-led chambers have adopted the NPVIC in New York (2011), Oklahoma (2014) and Arizona (2016) — but generally, Democrats have needed complete statehouse control to enact it into law. Which is where Democrats' shiny new trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin and Nevada come into play. What's next According to the Times, "lawmakers in key states said on Thursday that they had already begun having conversations this week about introducing legislation to join the agreement in the next session, and were hopeful that they would succeed ahead of 2028." But hopeful doesn't mean certain. One of the new trifecta states, Michigan, failed to get over the line during its previous Democratic trifecta, from 2023 to 2024 — and Nevada fell short in 2019 when its then-Democratic governor vetoed the compact amid fears it could diminish his small state's outsized influence over presidential elections. Virginia became the most recent state to join the compact after Democrats there won a trifecta in 2025. Republicans called the move an " unconstitutional assault on our democracy ," arguing it undermines the influence of Virginia voters. One major question is whether lawmakers will prioritize the national popular vote after campaigning in 2026 on more visceral issues like lowering the cost of living. "Time will tell," Clinton Anderson, a Democratic state assemblyman in Wisconsin, told the Times. "I want to make it a priority, but it's not the thing I heard on the doors I knocked." Another question is what might happen in the courts if the compact actually kicks in. Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller has argued that the NPVIC would be unconstitutional without congressional approval — which, in his view, is required under the Constitution's Compact Clause. "It's a very real possibility that enough states join this compact," Muller told the Times. But, he added, "there will be a lot of challenges."
